summary:
SPeace is a portrait-mode mobile app that brings an astronaut’s health information, space-weather risk and medical support into one place. It has seven sections: Reports (i-STAT blood tests), Ultrasound imaging, SP+ (an AI assistant that gives short, case-specific, temporary guidance), Your Doctor (chat and calls with an assigned doctor who also receives the reports and SP+ history), Data Zone (radiation and space-weather data), a green or red Peace score with an alert icon, and Settings.

It addresses the challenge of staying healthy far from Earth, where immediate medical help is limited. Astronauts get early warnings about conditions that affect the body, guidance while waiting for a doctor, and a doctor who can review everything.

This matters because deep-space missions face radiation, bone and muscle loss, and delayed communication. SPeace also creates skilled jobs for job seekers in Bahrain through its Bahraini medical team. We are also aiming to cooperate with Bahrain’s Al-Munther satellite team. Data Zone percentages are scaled against NASA reference values. This is a prototype, and its data is simulated.
details:
• tails, chronic conditions, allergies and current medications.
  • Reports and Ultrasound: these pages list dated results, show analysis progress and let the astronaut download or share a file.
  • SP+: the astronaut can type, attach files or photos, or record voice. Previous conversations are saved by date. SP+ replies with a likely cause, 3–4 numbered steps and when to call the doctor, and it gives an urgent message for emergencies. It never gives medicine doses.
  • Your Doctor: this is a WhatsApp-style chat with voice notes, photos, files, and voice and video call buttons.
  • Data Zone: each percentage is scaled against reference values from NASA sources, such as the Kp scale, solar wind speed range, the May 2024 solar particle event peak and ISS neutron dose rates. The Peace score is 100 minus the average of the other values, green at 50% or more and red below. The page raises a warning banner when a value gets high.
  • Settings: language (English or Arabic with right-to-left layout), light or dark mode, notifications, password change, and an editable list of current medications.

Benefits and intended impact

  • Astronauts see their health data and environmental risks together.
  • They get quick guidance while waiting for a doctor.
  • The doctor sees reports and the AI history in one place and can give feedback.
  • The intended impact is safer, more independent medical care on long missions.

Tools and technology

  • A single web app written in HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with no external libraries.
  • It was built and tested with Claude (Anthropic), and SP+ answers also use Claude when the app runs inside claude.ai.
  • Background research used NASA sources (DONKI, the CME Scoreboard, OMNIWeb, NASA Technical Reports Server papers and the ISS-RAD radiation measurements) and a risk and countermeasure document.
  • We used no physical hardware. The i-STAT and Ultrasound-2 devices, satellite feeds, doctor messaging and calls are simulated.

Creativity

  • A space-themed look with a nebula background, stars, a ringed planet and a heartbeat line that links space and medicine.
  • The Peace score turns many separate space-weather readings into one easy signal.
  • SP+ and the doctor work as a pair: the AI helps first, and the doctor reviews it afterward.
  • The owner controls the default color palette, in a theme block in the code.

Factors we considered

  • Mobile and portrait layout, with a formal look and light and dark modes.
  • Safety: no medication doses, clear emergency messages, and an honest note when a risk has no proven treatment.
  • Source quality: weaker sources, such as a student abstract, were flagged.
  • Privacy: account data stays on the user’s own device in this prototype.
  • Accessibility: English and Arabic with right-to-left layout.

Limits

  • This is a prototype, so reports, dates and Data Zone numbers are simulated.
  • The astronaut ID check only checks the format.
  • A real mission app would need live feeds from the devices and satellites, a secure server for accounts and doctor chat, and medical review of all guidance.
